newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. to take remains of Iraqi Scuds for study.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to take remains of Iraqi Scuds for study.

text.p: The United Nations plans to take the remains of missiles for study outside Iraq to help assess Baghdad's claims that all Scuds have been destroyed, a senior U.N. official said on Monday.

Goran R. Wallen, head of the Baghdad office of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) overseeing the elimination of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, said Iraq has maintained it destroyed the banned Scuds in 1991.
The commission has called on Baghdad to prove the missiles were destroyed. Rolf Ekeus, the U.N. commission chief, said last week Iraq was still concealing as many as 16 missiles.
"We are excavacating the (Scud) missiles, bringing them from sites where Iraq said it had destroyed them to Baghdad," Wallen told Reuters.
"We are intending to send them outside the country for scientific assessment," said Wallen, head of the Special Commission's Baghdad Monitoring and Verification Centre.
In 1992 Iraq gave the United Nations a list of hundreds of missiles, launch vehicles and other weapons it said it had destroyed and buried in July 1991.

Terms of the ceasefire that ended the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait ban Iraq from having missiles with a range greater than 150 km (94 miles) and the means to produce them. During the war Iraq fired scores of the Soviet-made Scuds at Saudi Arabia and Israel.
Wallen gave no details on the number of missiles to be excavated or where they would be moved for assessment.

The U.N. Security Council requires the commission to say Iraq no longer has banned weapons -- nuclear, chemical, biological and prohibited missiles -- before it will lift an embargo on Iraqi oil exports enforced since Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Ekeus said finding out what happened to the 16 missiles could lead to quick progress on other issues, such as chemical and biological arms.
Wallen also said 10 inspectors arrived in Baghdad on Monday to "tag' Iraq's Soviet-made Volga anti-aircraft missiles under an old agreement betweem the commission and the Iraqi authorities.

While anti-aircraft missiles are not banned under the ceasefire terms, U.N. experts want to document them if case they are later converted into surface-to-surface missiles with a range beyond that allowed.
